newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Haensch calls for crackdown on abuse of EP allowances.
newsitem.headline: Haensch calls for crackdown on abuse of EP allowances.

text.p: European Parliament President Klaus Haensch said on Thursday the system of Euro-MPs allowances, the butt of stinging criticism from inside and outside the assembly, should be reformed.

"Last night there was a consensus that these reforms would have to be continued," Haensch told a news conference after a specially convened meeting on Wednesday with the parliament's vice-presidents and political group leaders to discuss allegations that some MEPs were abusing the system.

Haensch said practical proposals for tightening up the system of members' daily allowances, travel expenses, personal assistants and their general statute would be put to the parliamentary leaders at the end of November.
MEPs abusing the rules would face sanctions, he warned.

"There has to be greater transparency about what MEPs receive, what they can receive and what they can't," added Haensch, saying this was to protect "the vast majority of colleagues who have always behaved absolutely correctly".

At present, MEPs can claim travel expenses without presenting their ticket as justification and they can sign an attendance register in Brussels or Strasbourg and then leave the building five minutes later.

The 8,937 Ecus a month an MEP is allowed for assistants is now paid directly to the latter, rather than to their boss, but there are no clear rules on MEPs' contributions to their aides' pensions and social security.

The possibilities of abuse are compounded by the fact that MEPs' salaries vary widely -- they earn the same as members of their home country's national parliament -- because the Council of Ministers has failed for many years to agree to a statute for MEPs.

As a result, some lower paid members try to fiddle their allowances to make up the difference, Claudia Roth, the president of the Green group and an outspoken critic of the current system, told Reuters.

"This was mentioned several times last night. I said I am sure we have to find a way to be more equal -- we are doing the same job -- but we cannot take the travel expenses system for this," she insisted.
Roth said she thought Haensch genuinely wanted reform but that he was trying to make compromises with truculent colleagues who wanted to maintain the status quo.
Haensch told reporters it was necessary to close the gap between travel refunds and the actual costs incurred by MEPs but argued that this was not as straighforward as it seemed.
"People who have further to go also have to spend more and take more time. It's not just the cost of the ticket...If they do not live near an airport they might have to stay overnight," he said.
Roth said she took issue with those who said producing actual receipts for expenses would be a costly administrative nightmare.

"If it costs money to guarantee a transparent system, we should do it. It's a question of credibility," she said, adding that other alternatives suggested at Wednesday's meeting would also entail extra administrative work.
Parliament sits in plenary session for seven days a month, five in Strasbourg and two in Brussels. Voting on European Union legislation takes place on only four and a half of these days.

MEPs' poor recond of attendance on the Friday plenary session in Strasbourg is an enduring bone of contention. Earlier this year, Irish Green Patricia McKenna pointed out the names on the attendance register bore no relation to the handful of deputies still in the chamber.
But Haensch said he did not object to MEPs claiming their attendance expenses and then using the Friday for other commitments, including travelling back to their constituencies.

"There are a large number of commitments involved other than sitting in the plenary," he told Reuters, adding that it was impossible to ensure the plenary did not clash with any engagements in the 15 member states.

Roth said she agreed with a proposal by Danish Christian Democrat Poul Shlueter to make members sign out at the end of each day in parliament as well as signing in, although she acknowledged there would then be the problem of deciding how many hours an MEP had to be in the building to be entitled to their daily allowance.

Haensch announced that proposals on a statute for MEPs' assistants were already before the European Commission and said he expected the parliament's rules committee to propose a statute for MEPs by the end of November, though the final decision would lie with the Council of Ministers.
Both Haensch and Roth said they wanted to see a standard rate of pay for MEPs bt acknowledged that changing the system presented genuine problems.

If Italian MEPs, who earn about four times as much as their Spanish colleagues, started receiving a lower salary than national deputies in Rome, only second class politicians would stand in European Parliament elections, Roth said.

By way of a compromise, she suggested MEPs should be paid equally by the EU, instead of by national governments, and the latter should provide an allowance, based on the national cost of living, to cover MEPs' office rental and other costs arising from work in their constituencies.
As for sanctions MEPs will face for abusing the system, Haensch said if caught they would be forced to pay the money back. But he did not foresee MEPs being forced to resign.
It was up to the political parties that put MEPs up for election and the people who voted for them to decide whether they were fit to stand for office again, he said.
